title: Cloud Marketplace Partner – Security collateral alignment (SOC 2, shared responsibility, listing requirements)
summary: AsterCloud Marketplace and Redwood aligned on the security collateral required for a marketplace listing and co-sell motion. Topics included: approved SOC 2 language and how to handle gated evidence requests (under NDA), ISO 27001 “alignment” wording (avoid certification claims), a shared responsibility model for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments, data retention/residency language (no overpromises), and audit logging/SSO/RBAC statements suitable for the listing page. The group agreed on a review workflow: Redwood Security/GRC owns factual security claims; Product Marketing owns messaging; Partnerships owns final packaging for the marketplace submission. Action items include Redwood delivering a short “security & trust” blurb + shared responsibility table, and AsterCloud providing their listing questionnaire and required template sections.
topics: Marketplace listing security questionnaire + required collateral
Shared responsibility model language by deployment mode
SOC 2: what can be stated publicly vs provided under NDA
SSO/SAML/SCIM, RBAC, and audit log export statements
Review workflow + versioning for approved language
questions: Can Redwood state “SOC 2 compliant” on the public marketplace page, or does it need to say “SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA”?
What is the most defensible way to describe ISO 27001 posture without implying certification?
Do customers have configurable retention controls in Hosted, and how should that be phrased without promising custom retention on all plans?
Is audit log export to customer SIEM available across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, and what are the limitations (fields/retention/destinations)?
How should the shared responsibility section address customer-managed networking and key management in Private/VPC deployments?
What is Redwood’s official stance on using customer data to train models, and how should that be written for a marketplace listing?
action_items: Camila Reyes (Redwood) - Draft marketplace-friendly “Security & Trust” copy block (150–250 words) + proof points per deployment mode; include SOC 2 and ISO language guardrails - Due 2025-10-27
Olga Petrov (Redwood) - Provide approved SOC 2 phrasing for public listing and gated evidence request workflow (NDA, turnaround) - Due 2025-10-27
Marcus Lin (Redwood) - Draft 1-page shared responsibility summary (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) with explicit boundaries (customer VPC/KMS) - Due 2025-10-29
Tomás Ribeiro (AsterCloud) - Send AsterCloud marketplace security questionnaire template + required sections/character limits - Due 2025-10-24
Elena Park (AsterCloud) - Confirm whether AsterCloud requires pen test frequency disclosure on listing page or only in private questionnaire - Due 2025-10-24
Jordan Blake (Redwood) - Set up follow-up review meeting with Partnerships + Security/GRC to approve final submission packet - Due 2025-10-30
next_steps: AsterCloud to share listing security questionnaire template and any required “shared responsibility” boilerplate.
Redwood to deliver approved short-form security copy, shared responsibility summary, and link to evidence request process for SOC 2 report under NDA.
Schedule 30-minute redline session to finalize the marketplace submission text and confirm internal approvers (Security/GRC + Marketing).
After approval, Partnerships submits listing packet and tracks any reviewer feedback/questions from AsterCloud.
transcript:
Meeting: Cloud Marketplace Partner – Security collateral alignment (SOC 2, shared responsibility, listing requirements)
Date/time: 2025-10-22 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 53 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Jordan Blake, Camila Reyes, Olga Petrov, Marcus Lin, Markus Klein
AsterCloud Marketplace: Tomás Ribeiro, Elena Park, Sanjay Iyer

---
Auto-generated notes (Fireflies)
Summary: Partner and Redwood aligned on marketplace security collateral, shared responsibility wording, SOC 2 / ISO language, and review workflow.
Action items: See action items section.

---

[00:00] Jordan Blake: Hey everyone. Thanks for making the time. This is Jordan from Redwood. Goal today is to align on what security collateral AsterCloud needs for the marketplace listing, and make sure we’re using approved language. Camila from Product Marketing is here, Olga from GRC, Marcus from Security Eng, Markus from Solutions Engineering.

[00:19] Tomás Ribeiro: Great. Hi all. Tomás, marketplace PM. We’re trying to get your listing into our “AI & Data” category, but security review is the gating item for the publish step.

[00:29] Elena Park: Elena, partner security. I handle the security questionnaire and the content checks. We’ve had issues with vendors over-claiming, so we’re trying to standardize language.

[00:39] Sanjay Iyer: Sanjay, compliance. I’ll probably ask the annoying ISO questions.

[00:44] Jordan Blake: (laughs) That’s why we brought Olga.

[00:47] Camila Reyes: Hi everyone.

[00:50] Olga Petrov: Hello.

[00:51] Marcus Lin: Hey.

[00:52] Markus Klein: Hi folks.

[00:55] Jordan Blake: Cool. Tomás, do you want to start with the checklist from AsterCloud? What’s required on the public listing vs private packet?

[01:04] Tomás Ribeiro: Sure. There’s basically two layers. First is the public marketplace page: a security section, data handling, residency if applicable, and support SLAs. Second is a questionnaire we run internally for “verified” listings—SOC 2 evidence, incident response policy confirmation, pen test cadence, things like that.

[01:22] Elena Park: And for the public page we don’t want you attaching PDFs. We want short, plain language, no marketing fluff. Like “SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA” versus “best-in-class security.”

[01:35] Camila Reyes: That’s helpful, thank you.

[01:37] Jordan Blake: On our side, we’re actively refreshing our enterprise security kit, so we want to make sure the marketplace copy doesn’t diverge. The biggest risk is different claims in different places.

[01:49] Sanjay Iyer: Exactly.

[01:51] Jordan Blake: Maybe we start with the big three: SOC 2, ISO, and shared responsibility across deployment modes.

[02:00] Elena Park: Works.

[02:02] Olga Petrov: For SOC 2, our standard is: we do not publish the report publicly. We can say we have a SOC 2 Type II report and it’s available to customers/partners under NDA upon request.

[02:14] Elena Park: Is it okay to say “SOC 2 compliant” on the public listing?

[02:18] Olga Petrov: We avoid “compliant” because it can be interpreted as continuously compliant or certified. We typically say: “Redwood has completed a SOC 2 Type II audit; report available under NDA.”

[02:30] Camila Reyes: We can also add “covering security, availability, and confidentiality” if that’s accurate, but we should keep it tight.

[02:36] Olga Petrov: Right—only if those trust principles are in scope. I can provide the exact approved sentence.

[02:44] Sanjay Iyer: Good. For ISO 27001, do you have certification?

[02:48] Olga Petrov: We are not claiming ISO 27001 certification publicly. We can speak to alignment of our information security program with ISO 27001 control themes, but we need to be careful—no implication of certification.

[03:02] Elena Park: So wording like “follows ISO 27001 best practices” is okay?

[03:07] Olga Petrov: “Aligned with” or “mapped to” is better than “follows.” We typically say “Our program is aligned with ISO 27001 control objectives” and stop there.

[03:18] Sanjay Iyer: Great. I’m going to ask later for the mapping, but that can be in the private packet.

[03:23] Olga Petrov: Yes, under NDA we can share more detail, depending on the request.

[03:29] Jordan Blake: On shared responsibility: Redwood has Hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private deployments (VPC/on-prem). The boundary is different per mode, and we want that spelled out clearly.

[03:41] Markus Klein: Yeah. For Hosted, Redwood manages the infrastructure, runtime, patching, and the serving stack. Customers manage their application integration, prompts, and their users. For Dedicated, it’s still Redwood-managed infrastructure but isolated capacity, and for Private it’s more customer-managed networking and sometimes customer-managed keys, depending.

[04:03] Elena Park: Okay, but the listing needs something crisp like a table. “Redwood is responsible for X, customer is responsible for Y.”

[04:11] Marcus Lin: We can draft a one-pager. But I want to avoid saying “customer is responsible for patching” if we don’t have a consistent model. In Private, for example, if it’s on-prem, the customer might manage host patching. In VPC, it depends on the deployment pattern.

[04:29] Tomás Ribeiro: Understood. Even a “varies by deployment” note is fine, but it needs to be explicit.

[04:35] Camila Reyes: We can keep the public listing high-level and link to a “shared responsibility overview” doc that’s gated or partner-only.

[04:42] Elena Park: For the public listing, links are okay if they’re stable and not behind login. For gated evidence, it’s okay to say “contact us.”

[04:52] Jordan Blake: Got it.

[04:54] Elena Park: Another big topic is data handling. Specifically: do you retain prompts? for how long? and do you train on customer data?

[05:05] Markus Klein: We get that question every call.

[05:07] Olga Petrov: For training: our approved statement is that we do not use customer inputs/outputs to train foundation models without explicit permission. There’s nuance with operational data and abuse monitoring, but we can provide the exact language.

[05:22] Elena Park: The marketplace page has a checkbox “vendor trains on customer data: yes/no.” We need a crisp answer.

[05:28] Olga Petrov: Then answer should be “No” with a footnote pointing to the policy statement.

[05:33] Marcus Lin: And we should add “unless customer opts in” because otherwise you’re blocking future optional programs.

[05:40] Camila Reyes: We can say “No (unless explicitly authorized by the customer).”

[05:45] Elena Park: That works.

[05:47] Sanjay Iyer: Now retention. For listing we need: “How long does the service store customer content?” and “How long are logs stored?”

[05:56] Markus Klein: This is where it varies by deployment and plan. Hosted has default retention windows for logs, and some controls for deletion. Dedicated and Private are more customizable.

[06:10] Marcus Lin: Also we should separate content from logs. People mix “prompt retention” with “request logs.”

[06:16] Olga Petrov: Exactly. We can provide language like: customer content is processed to provide the service; any storage is limited and configurable depending on deployment; operational logs are retained for security and reliability for a defined period.

[06:33] Elena Park: Can you give numbers? Like 30 days, 90 days?

[06:37] Olga Petrov: We should not put numbers on the public listing unless we are certain they are universally true. If there are plan-dependent options, we can say “configurable retention options, including shorter retention,” and refer to the detailed doc.

[06:53] Jordan Blake: That aligns with our internal policy—avoid exact days in public collateral unless it’s locked.

[06:58] Tomás Ribeiro: For our listing, we allow “default retention: X” plus “configurable.” But if you don’t want to give X, then “varies by plan” is acceptable.

[07:08] Camila Reyes: We can do “Retention controls vary by deployment mode and customer configuration; details available on request.” That’s likely safest.

[07:17] Elena Park: Okay. Data residency is the next one. Can you say you support EU residency?

[07:24] Markus Klein: We have EU regions for Hosted and Dedicated depending on availability, and for Private you can deploy in customer VPC in their chosen region. But we need to be careful about what data stays where—metadata, support access, etc.

[07:41] Marcus Lin: Also, “residency” is not the same as “sovereignty.” We can say data is processed in the selected region, with operational exceptions (support) under strict controls.

[07:52] Olga Petrov: And only if true. The approved phrasing we’ve used is: “Customers can select the region for processing; data residency commitments are contractual and subject to product constraints.”

[08:05] Elena Park: Understood. Our listing has “Supports EU region: yes/no.” So likely “Yes, with region selection,” and then the caveat.

[08:14] Jordan Blake: For the listing page, we can say “Regional deployments available (including EU).” And for Private: “deployable in customer-managed VPC/on-prem.”

[08:27] Tomás Ribeiro: Great.

[08:29] Elena Park: Switching topics: access controls. SSO/SAML/SCIM, RBAC. We need to know what’s in the product vs “sales says it exists.”

[08:41] Markus Klein: We support SSO via SAML for the console for enterprise plans, SCIM provisioning for certain plans, and RBAC roles. There’s some nuance about which surfaces—console vs API keys.

[08:55] Marcus Lin: And audit logs. You’ll want a statement about audit log events and export.

[09:01] Elena Park: Yes, specifically: “Can customers export audit logs to SIEM?”

[09:06] Marcus Lin: We support exporting audit events to customer destinations in certain deployments—commonly to an S3 bucket or a webhook-style sink. SIEM integration is usually via the customer pulling from that destination.

[09:20] Elena Park: So not a direct “Splunk app” built-in.

[09:23] Marcus Lin: Not as a first-class one-click, no. We should not claim that.

[09:28] Camila Reyes: So the public copy should say “Audit logging available; export supported via standard integrations” and avoid naming a specific SIEM unless we have a validated integration.

[09:39] Markus Klein: Exactly. We can mention common patterns like “S3 or customer-managed log pipeline,” but keep it accurate.

[09:49] Sanjay Iyer: Pen test: do you do annual external penetration testing?

[09:54] Marcus Lin: We do regular testing and vulnerability scanning. The frequency and scope are internal, and we can share a high-level statement. We should avoid giving a strict cadence on a public listing.

[10:08] Olga Petrov: We can answer in the private questionnaire under NDA with the approved language from our security program statement.

[10:16] Elena Park: Okay. The marketplace page doesn’t require frequency, but our internal “verified listing” does.

[10:23] Jordan Blake: Great. That’s a good division: public page minimal, private packet more detail.

[10:29] Tomás Ribeiro: One more: subcontractors / subprocessors. Do you have a list you can share?

[10:36] Olga Petrov: We maintain a subprocessor list. Publicly we can share the list or provide it during contracting, depending. Typically we provide a canonical link or upon request.

[10:48] Elena Park: For our process, a link is best, but it needs to be stable.

[10:52] Camila Reyes: We can coordinate with our docs owner to ensure the link stays stable, or provide it as part of the partner packet.

[11:00] Jordan Blake: Let’s talk workflow. AsterCloud wants content. Redwood wants to make sure it’s approved. Who reviews on your side?

[11:09] Elena Park: I do security content review. Sanjay signs off on compliance statements. Tomás does the product/UX of the listing.

[11:18] Jordan Blake: On Redwood side, for any security claim: Olga for compliance language, Marcus for technical controls. Camila for messaging. I’ll own packaging and submission timeline.

[11:31] Tomás Ribeiro: Great. We can work async over a doc.

[11:34] Camila Reyes: We usually do it in a single doc with redlines and a “last reviewed” date. We also keep a change log so sales doesn’t copy old text.

[11:44] Elena Park: That’s good. Our reviewer team will ask “when was this last validated.”

[11:50] Markus Klein: Also, you mentioned character limits. Do you have those?

[11:55] Tomás Ribeiro: Yep. Public listing security blurb is 1,500 characters max. Data handling section is 800 characters. “Compliance” section is a set of checkboxes plus a 400-character note.

[12:10] Camila Reyes: That’s helpful. We’ll draft within those limits.

[12:14] Jordan Blake: Can you send the template after this call?

[12:17] Tomás Ribeiro: Yes.

[12:19] Jordan Blake: Great.

[12:21] (crosstalk)
[12:22] Elena Park: Sorry, one more question—encryption and KMS. For listing we need in-transit, at-rest, and if customer can use their own keys.

[12:33] Marcus Lin: In transit is TLS. At rest is encrypted. For customer-managed keys: in Private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS, and in some cases dedicated environments. But we should phrase it as “supports customer-managed key integrations in certain deployment modes.”

[12:49] Markus Klein: Yeah, and it’s often a contract/config choice, not a toggle for self-serve Hosted.

[12:56] Elena Park: So for Hosted, just say “encryption at rest/in transit.” For Private: “optional customer-managed KMS.”

[13:03] Olga Petrov: With the boundary: who owns and controls keys depends on deployment. We can draft that.

[13:10] Sanjay Iyer: Also: do you support HSM?

[13:13] Marcus Lin: We can support HSM-backed KMS depending on the cloud provider. But again, avoid “we provide HSM” in Hosted.

[13:22] Camila Reyes: We’ll keep it “supports integrations with customer key management systems (KMS/HSM) in Private deployments” if that’s accurate.

[13:30] Marcus Lin: Yes, “KMS/HSM integrations” is better.

[13:33] Jordan Blake: Okay.

[13:35] Elena Park: What about incident response: do you have a breach notification policy? Our questionnaire asks “notify within X hours.”

[13:44] Olga Petrov: We have an incident response program and we have standard contractual terms for notification. We should not commit to a number in marketplace collateral. In contracting, we can negotiate within reason.

[13:58] Jordan Blake: Right, that becomes legal.

[14:01] Tomás Ribeiro: For public listing, we just need “has IR program: yes.”

[14:06] Elena Park: For verified listing, we’ll ask your standard language.

[14:10] Olga Petrov: Under NDA we can provide the high-level overview; contractual commitments go through Legal.

[14:18] Jordan Blake: Great.

[14:20] (brief pause)

[14:22] Jordan Blake: Maybe let’s go through the public listing sections one by one and decide what goes where.

[14:28] Tomás Ribeiro: Sure.

[14:30] Jordan Blake: Section 1: Security overview. Camila, I think we can say: “Redwood provides a developer-first LLM inference platform with hosted, dedicated, and private deployment options; security controls include encryption in transit and at rest, role-based access control, SSO/SAML, audit logging, and ongoing vulnerability management.” Something like that.

[14:49] Camila Reyes: Yes, but I’d prefer to list controls that are true across the deployments, and then a “capabilities vary” line. We can do bullet-ish sentences.

[14:58] Elena Park: Bullets are okay, but no more than like six.

[15:03] Marcus Lin: Make sure “SSO” is not implied for every plan if it’s enterprise only.

[15:08] Camila Reyes: Good point. We can say “Enterprise features include SSO/SAML and SCIM.”

[15:15] Markus Klein: And RBAC applies to the console, and API keys are separate. That nuance may be too much for the listing though.

[15:22] Elena Park: For listing, broad is okay. For the private packet, we’ll want the nuance.

[15:28] Jordan Blake: Section 2: Compliance. SOC 2 statement, plus “report available under NDA.” ISO alignment optional line.

[15:37] Sanjay Iyer: Please don’t put ISO unless you add the caveat.

[15:41] Olga Petrov: Agree. We can do: “SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA. Redwood’s security program is aligned with ISO 27001 control objectives.” That’s it.

[15:54] Elena Park: Great.

[15:56] Jordan Blake: Section 3: Data handling. “No training on customer data without permission.” “Retention varies.” “Region selection available.”

[16:05] Markus Klein: And mention private deployments for regulated customers.

[16:10] Tomás Ribeiro: Yes, that helps our buyer persona.

[16:13] Jordan Blake: Section 4: Shared responsibility. On the public listing, maybe just a short “Redwood manages infrastructure for Hosted and Dedicated; Private deployments support customer-managed networking and key management.”

[16:27] Marcus Lin: Plus: “Customers are responsible for their applications and access policies.”

[16:32] Elena Park: That’s fine. In the private packet, we’ll want the actual table.

[16:38] Jordan Blake: Great.

[16:40] (transition)

[16:41] Elena Park: One thing: We’ve had vendor listings that say “supports data deletion on request” and then they can’t do it. Do you support deletion?

[16:51] Markus Klein: We support deletion processes. Exact behavior depends on what’s stored and for how long. In Hosted, if content isn’t stored long-term, deletion is more about logs and any saved artifacts.

[17:05] Marcus Lin: Also backups. People forget to mention backups, and then it’s a gotcha.

[17:09] Olga Petrov: Our approved language usually says “Deletion requests are supported per contract; certain security logs may be retained for a defined period.” We can provide that.

[17:20] Elena Park: Perfect. We just need you not to imply “immediate deletion from all systems everywhere.”

[17:26] Olga Petrov: We won’t.

[17:28] Tomás Ribeiro: Another: do you do HIPAA? Some of our buyers are healthcare.

[17:33] Jordan Blake: We can support regulated deployments, but we should be careful. We can say we can sign BAAs in certain configurations and with Private/Dedicated, subject to review.

[17:45] Olga Petrov: Yes, that’s contractual. Not a default statement on marketplace.

[17:50] Elena Park: Fine. We won’t put HIPAA on the public listing unless it’s official.

[17:56] Jordan Blake: Great.

[18:00] Sanjay Iyer: For the verified listing, we’ll ask: “Provide SOC 2 report,” “Describe vulnerability management,” “Provide subprocessor list,” “Describe encryption,” and “Describe audit logs.”

[18:12] Marcus Lin: For audit logs, we can provide an event taxonomy summary: authentication events, API key changes, role changes, resource changes. Maybe not all details, but enough.

[18:24] Elena Park: Do you have an audit log retention policy?

[18:28] Olga Petrov: We have default retention and configurable options. We’ll share the exact ranges in the private packet; again, public listing should avoid exact days.

[18:40] Tomás Ribeiro: Understood.

[18:42] (brief pause)

[18:44] Jordan Blake: Let’s confirm how we exchange the gated stuff. AsterCloud—do you have an NDA framework for partners?

[18:51] Tomás Ribeiro: Yes. For verified listing, we can execute a partner NDA through our standard workflow.

[18:58] Olga Petrov: Great. That’s a requirement for sharing the SOC 2 Type II report.

[19:04] Elena Park: For our internal reviewers, we don’t need the full report in the ticket; a secure link is fine.

[19:10] Olga Petrov: We can provide access via our evidence request process. It’s basically: request comes in, NDA verified, then time-bound access to a folder or secure share.

[19:22] Jordan Blake: We’ll keep the process consistent with what we do for customers, so it doesn’t become a new one-off.

[19:29] Camila Reyes: And we’ll keep the listing copy aligned with that: “Report available under NDA upon request.”

[19:36] Elena Park: Great.

[19:38] (crosstalk)
[19:39] Markus Klein: Quick nuance: when we say “Private,” we mean either VPC deployment or on-prem package. Do you want both mentioned?

[19:47] Tomás Ribeiro: Yes, but if on-prem is limited availability, don’t oversell it.

[19:52] Markus Klein: It’s available for regulated customers, but not self-serve. We can say “VPC and on-prem options available for regulated workloads.”

[20:02] Marcus Lin: “Available” is fine as long as we don’t say “any customer can do on-prem tomorrow.”

[20:07] Camila Reyes: We can word it as “Private deployments are available, including VPC and on-prem options, subject to engagement and contract.”

[20:16] Elena Park: Perfect.

[20:18] Jordan Blake: Awesome.

[20:20] (topic shift)

[20:21] Elena Park: One more: support access. Do your engineers access customer data when troubleshooting?

[20:28] Marcus Lin: Support access is controlled and logged. We generally avoid accessing customer content unless necessary and authorized, and we prefer customers provide redacted samples.

[20:41] Olga Petrov: We can provide a standard statement about least privilege, approval, and audit logging for support access.

[20:50] Elena Park: Great. Include that in the private packet.

[20:54] Jordan Blake: OK.

[20:56] Tomás Ribeiro: Timeline wise, we want to publish in November. That means we need final public copy by end of next week.

[21:05] Jordan Blake: That’s doable if we get the template today/tomorrow.

[21:09] Camila Reyes: We can draft within 48 hours after template.

[21:12] Olga Petrov: I can review within a day.

[21:15] Marcus Lin: Same.

[21:17] Elena Park: Great.

[21:19] (silence)

[21:21] Jordan Blake: Before we wrap, any other required statements? Sometimes marketplaces ask for “Data used for ad targeting” or “Sell data.”

[21:29] Tomás Ribeiro: Yes. There’s a privacy section: “Do you sell personal data?” and “Do you use data for advertising?”

[21:36] Olga Petrov: The answer should be “No.” We can provide the exact phrasing.

[21:41] Camila Reyes: And we can align it with our privacy policy language.

[21:46] Elena Park: Great.

[21:48] Sanjay Iyer: Also, do you have a DPA?

[21:50] Jordan Blake: Yes, standard DPA available during contracting.

[21:54] Olga Petrov: We can say “DPA available upon request.”

[21:58] Elena Park: Okay.

[22:00] Jordan Blake: Cool. I think we have what we need.

[22:03] Tomás Ribeiro: Actually, quick competitor context: AsterCloud has other LLM vendors listing. Reviewers sometimes ask “are you similar to OpenAI or Bedrock.”

[22:12] Jordan Blake: We can position as inference platform, not model owner. But that’s marketing; security-wise it shouldn’t matter.

[22:20] Camila Reyes: For listing, we keep it factual, avoid comparisons.

[22:23] Elena Park: Appreciate that.

[22:26] Jordan Blake: Great. Let’s recap next steps.

[22:29] Jordan Blake: Tomás, you’ll send the template and character limits. Elena, you’ll confirm whether the pen test frequency is required publicly or only in verified packet. On Redwood side: Camila drafts the public security blurb; Olga provides approved SOC 2 + ISO language; Marcus drafts a shared responsibility one-pager/table for the verified packet.

[22:52] Elena Park: Sounds good.

[22:54] Tomás Ribeiro: Yes.

[22:55] Sanjay Iyer: Works.

[22:58] Jordan Blake: We’ll schedule a 30-minute redline session next week to lock it. Thanks everyone.

[23:05] Camila Reyes: Thanks.

[23:06] Olga Petrov: Thank you.

[23:07] Marcus Lin: Thanks.

[23:08] Markus Klein: Appreciate it.

[23:10] Tomás Ribeiro: Bye.

[23:11] Elena Park: Bye.
